tip.title: padres = parents
tip.body: Spanish uses the masculine plural for mixed groups: los padres means "the parents" (not only fathers), los hermanos can mean "brothers and sisters", and los abuelos "grandparents". So ¿Tienes hermanos? simply asks "Do you have siblings?". In everyday speech people say mamá and papá, with the stress on the last syllable.

phrases.t: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
phrases.n: I have a brother and a sister.
Do you have brothers and sisters?
phrases.note: hermanos covers siblings of either sex.

phrases.n: I'm an only child. (man; a woman says hija única)

phrases.note: hijos = sons, or children of either sex.

lines.name: Lucía
lines.n: Who's this?

lines.t: Esta es mi madre, y este es mi padre.
lines.n: This is my mother, and this is my father.

lines.name: Lucía
lines.n: They look lovely! Do you have siblings?
Yes, I have a sister. And you?

lessons.title: What are they like?
lessons.goal: Describe how people look and what they're like.

tip.title: Adjectives match the person
tip.body: Adjectives ending in -o change to -a for a woman: mi hermano es alto, mi hermana es alta. Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant usually stay the same: amable, joven. For looks, use tener: tiene el pelo corto (he/she has short hair), tiene los ojos verdes. Mayor is the polite word for "old"; viejo can sound rude about people.

phrases.t: Mi hermano es bajo y delgado.
phrases.n: My brother is short and slim.

phrases.t: Mi abuela es mayor pero muy activa.
phrases.n: My grandmother is elderly but very active.

phrases.note: For a woman: joven y divertida.
In Latin America also: usa lentes.

lines.name: Diego
lines.t: ¿Viene tu hermana a la fiesta? ¿Cómo es?
lines.n: Is your sister coming to the party? What's she like?

lines.t: Sí, viene. Es alta y tiene el pelo largo.
lines.n: Yes, she's coming. She's tall and has long hair.

lines.name: Diego
lines.n: And is she nice?
Very nice and very fun!

lines.name: Diego
lines.n: Cool, great!

Say your sister is tall and nice.

tip.title: Pets are part of the family
tip.body: Mascota means pet. Perro (dog) and gato (cat) change to perra and gata for females. Spanish uses the same verb for pets as for family: tengo un perro, tengo dos hermanos. Tiny animals often get a diminutive: perrito, gatito (doggy, kitty).

lines.n: What a cute little dog! What's his name?

lines.name: Javier
lines.t: Se llama Coco. Tiene dos años.
lines.n: He's called Coco. He's two years old.

lines.name: Javier
lines.n: Do you have pets?

lines.t: Sí, tengo dos gatos. Me encantan los animales.
lines.n: Yes, I have two cats. I love animals.

prompts.n: Ask someone if they have pets.

lessons.title: mi, tu, su: possessives
lessons.goal: Say whose family member it is.

tip.title: Possessives match the thing owned, not the owner
tip.body: mi (my), tu (your), su (his/her/your polite/their) add -s when the noun is plural: mi hermano, mis hermanos; su perro, sus perros. Nuestro (our) and vuestro (your, plural, Spain only) also change for gender: nuestra madre, nuestros abuelos. Note tu (your) has no accent; tú (you) does. Because su has many meanings, people add de … to be clear: el perro de Ana.

lessons.title: Sunday at grandma's
lessons.goal: Follow a family description at natural speed.

phrases.t: Los domingos comemos en casa de mi abuela.
phrases.n: On Sundays we have lunch at my grandmother's.
There are a lot of us.

story.title: A big family
story.intro: Valeria, from Guadalajara, tells her friend Carlos about her family lunch.

lines.name: Carlos
lines.n: Hey, Valeria, what are you doing on Sunday?

lines.name: Valeria
lines.t: Los domingos comemos en casa de mi abuela. Es una tradición.
lines.n: On Sundays we have lunch at my grandmother's. It's a tradition.

lines.name: Carlos
lines.n: And who goes?

lines.name: Valeria
lines.t: Mis papás, mi hermano mayor con su esposa, mis tíos y mis primos. ¡Somos muchos!
lines.n: My parents, my older brother with his wife, my aunt and uncle and my cousins. There are a lot of us!

lines.name: Carlos
lines.n: And your grandmother cooks for everyone?

lines.name: Valeria
lines.t: Sí, tiene setenta y cinco años y cocina muy rico. Mi hermana menor y yo la ayudamos.
lines.n: Yes, she's seventy-five and cooks really well. My younger sister and I help her.

lines.name: Carlos
lines.t: ¡Qué bonito! Yo solo veo a mi familia en Navidad.
lines.n: How lovely! I only see my family at Christmas.

choices.t: Mucho gusto, señora. Gracias por la invitación.

rude.t: ¡Ay, qué prisa! Primero cuéntame: ¿y tu familia?

lessons.title: Introduce your family

culture.title: Abuelos, primos and Sunday lunch
culture.body: In Spain and Latin America the family often means the extended family: grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins. Many families get together for a long lunch at the weekend, often at the grandparents' house, and grandparents frequently help look after the children. Young adults often live with their parents for longer than in many English-speaking countries. Everyone says mamá and papá, and in Mexico mis papás means "my parents". People also have two surnames: the first from the father and the second from the mother, traditionally.

phrases.note: mis papás = my parents (very common in Latin America).

phrases.t: Veo a mis abuelos los domingos.
phrases.n: I see my grandparents on Sundays.
